summary: Iranian-market conventions. Applications commonly arrive as a رزومه (resume) attached to a covering message on job boards, and increasingly through company application forms.

photo.note: A formal photo is common on Iranian resumes and appears more often than in Western markets. It is optional; many companies and all ATS pipelines work better without one.

personalInfo.note: National ID (کد ملی) and a full home address are personal data with no recruiting value at the screening stage. They stay disabled until you switch them on deliberately. Military-service status is handled as its own section because some employers do ask for it.

page.note: One to two pages is typical for most roles; academic and senior engineering CVs may run longer.

notes: Large technology employers and international companies recruiting in Iran frequently use English-language ATS pipelines; keep a single-column, text-based version for those.
Persian text is laid out right-to-left with correct letter joining, so the file stays readable in every viewer.
Persian resumes are usually written in a formal register using the past tense for completed roles.
Persian and English CVs are both accepted; English is expected for multinationals and for remote roles.

advisories.text: Functional (skills-first) resumes are uncommon in Iran; the reverse-chronological structure is what most reviewers expect.
Military-service status is requested by some employers as a separate field. It is available as an optional section and is never added automatically.

The Persian (Jalali) calendar is the local norm, but most job boards and all international ATS parsers expect Gregorian dates. Use Jalali for domestic applications and Gregorian for anything crossing a border.
